**Gaius Julius Caesar**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-4) (12 or 13 July 100 BC – 15 March 44 BC) was a Roman general, statesman, and author who was the [dictator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_dictator "Roman dictator") of the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") almost continuously from 49 BC until [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Julius_Caesar "Assassination of Julius Caesar") in 44 BC. A member of the [First Triumvirate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Triumvirate "First Triumvirate"), he led the Roman armies through the [Gallic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallic_Wars "Gallic Wars") and defeated his political rival [Pompey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey "Pompey") in [Caesar's civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar's_civil_war "Caesar's civil war"). He consolidated power and was titled as _[dictator perpetuo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictator\_perpetuo "Dictator perpetuo")_ in 44 BC, helping create the [political conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Roman_Republic "Crisis of the Roman Republic") that led to the collapse of the Roman Republic and the emergence of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"). For his role in these events, he is regarded as one of history's most influential figures.

In 60 BC, Caesar, [Crassus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crassus "Crassus"), and Pompey formed the First Triumvirate, an informal political alliance that dominated [Roman politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_politics "Roman politics") for several years. Their attempts to amass political power were opposed by many in the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate "Roman Senate"), including [Cato the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cato_the_Younger "Cato the Younger") with the private support of [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero "Cicero"). Caesar rose to become one of the most powerful politicians in the Roman Republic through a string of military victories in the Gallic Wars, completed by 51 BC, which greatly expanded Roman territory. During this time, he [invaded Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar's_invasions_of_Britain "Caesar's invasions of Britain") and [built a bridge across the Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar's_Rhine_bridges "Caesar's Rhine bridges"). These achievements, along with the loyalty of his veteran army, threatened to eclipse the standing of Pompey. The alliance between Caesar and Pompey slowly broke down and, by 50 BC, Pompey had realigned himself with the Senate. With his command expiring and the Gallic Wars largely concluded, the Senate ordered Caesar to relinquish his military command and return to Rome. In early January 49 BC, Caesar openly defied the Senate by [crossing the Rubicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_the_Rubicon "Crossing the Rubicon") and marching towards Rome at the head of an army. This act began Caesar's civil war, which he won, leaving him in a position of near-unchallenged power and influence in 45 BC.

After assuming control of government and pardoning many of his enemies, Caesar carried out various reforms and public works. He created the [Julian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_calendar "Julian calendar") to replace the republican lunisolar calendar, reduced the size of the [grain dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cura_annonae "Cura annonae"), settled his veterans in new overseas colonies, greatly increased the size of the Senate, and extended citizenship to communities in Spain and what is now northern Italy. In early 44 BC, he was proclaimed "dictator in perpetuity". Fearful of his power, his domination of the state, and the possibility that he might make himself king, a group of senators led by [Brutus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutus "Brutus") and [Cassius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Cassius_Longinus "Gaius Cassius Longinus") assassinated Caesar on the [Ides of March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ides_of_March "Ides of March") (15 March) 44 BC. A new [series of civil wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Triumvirate#Triumviral_period "Second Triumvirate") broke out and the [constitutional government of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Roman_Republic "Constitution of the Roman Republic") was never fully restored. Caesar's great-nephew and adoptive heir [Octavian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_life_of_Augustus "Early life of Augustus"), later known as [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus"), [rose to sole power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rise_of_Augustus "Rise of Augustus") after [defeating his opponents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_Actium "War of Actium") thirteen years later. Octavian then set about consolidating [his power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Augustus "Reign of Augustus"), transforming the Republic into the Roman Empire as its [first emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_emperor "Roman emperor").

Caesar was an accomplished author and commentator; much of his life is known through his own accounts of his military campaigns. Other contemporary sources include the letters and speeches of Cicero and the historical writings of [Sallust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sallust "Sallust"). Later biographies of Caesar by [Suetonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suetonius "Suetonius") and [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch "Plutarch") are also important sources. Caesar is considered by many historians to be one of the greatest military commanders in history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-5) His [cognomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognomen "Cognomen") subsequently became a synonym for emperor; the title _[Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar\_(title) "Caesar (title)")_ was used throughout the Roman Empire, and gave rise to modern derivatives such as [Kaiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaiser "Kaiser") and [Tsar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar "Tsar"). He has [frequently appeared in literary and artistic works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_depictions_of_Julius_Caesar "Cultural depictions of Julius Caesar").

## Early life and career

Gaius Julius Caesar was born into a [patrician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrician_(ancient_Rome) "Patrician (ancient Rome)") family, the _[gens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gens "Gens")[Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia\_gens "Julia gens")_, on 12 or 13 July 100 BC.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-6) The family claimed to have immigrated to Rome from [Alba Longa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alba_Longa "Alba Longa") during the seventh century BC after the third [king of Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Rome "King of Rome"), [Tullus Hostilius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tullus_Hostilius "Tullus Hostilius"), took and destroyed their city. The family also claimed descent from [Julus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascanius "Ascanius"), the son of [Aeneas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneas "Aeneas") and founder of Alba Longa. Given that Aeneas was a son of [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_(mythology) "Venus (mythology)"), this made the clan divine. This genealogy had not yet taken its final form by the first century, but the clan's claimed descent from Venus was well established in public consciousness.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9333-7) There is no evidence that Caesar himself was born by [Caesarian section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesarian_section "Caesarian section"); such operations entailed the death of the mother, but [Caesar's mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar's_mother "Caesar's mother") lived for decades after his birth and no ancient sources record any difficulty with the birth.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200635-8)

Despite their ancient pedigree, the Julii Caesares were not especially politically influential during the middle republic. The first person known to have had the [cognomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognomen "Cognomen")_Caesar_ was a praetor in 208 BC during the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War"). The family's first consul was in 157 BC, though their political fortunes had recovered in the early first century, producing two consuls in 91 and 90 BC.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-9)[Caesar's homonymous father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar's_homonymous_father "Caesar's homonymous father") was moderately successful politically. He married [Aurelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelia_(mother_of_Caesar) "Aurelia (mother of Caesar)"), a member of the politically influential [Aurelii Cottae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelii_Cottae "Aurelii Cottae"), producing – along with Caesar – two daughters. Buoyed by his own marriage and the marriage of [his sister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(wife_of_Marius) "Julia (wife of Marius)") to the extremely influential [Gaius Marius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Marius "Gaius Marius"), he also served on the [Saturninian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Appuleius_Saturninus "Lucius Appuleius Saturninus") land commission in 103 BC and was elected praetor some time between 92 and 85 BC; he served as proconsular governor of [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia_(Roman_province) "Asia (Roman province)") for two years, likely 91–90 BC.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-10)

### Life under Sulla and military service

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Q._Pompeius_Rufus%2C_denarius%2C_54_BC%2C_RRC_434-1_%28Sulla_only%29.jpg/250px-Q._Pompeius_Rufus%2C_denarius%2C_54_BC%2C_RRC_434-1_%28Sulla_only%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Q._Pompeius_Rufus,_denarius,_54_BC,_RRC_434-1_(Sulla_only).jpg)

Sulla, depicted on the [obverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obverse_and_reverse "Obverse and reverse") of a [denarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denarius "Denarius") minted by [Quintus Pompeius Rufus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Pompeius_Rufus_(grandson_of_Sulla) "Quintus Pompeius Rufus (grandson of Sulla)") in 54 BC. Sulla took the city in 82 BC, purged his political enemies, and instituted [new constitutional reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_reforms_of_Sulla "Constitutional reforms of Sulla").

Caesar's father did not seek a consulship during the domination of [Lucius Cornelius Cinna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Cornelius_Cinna "Lucius Cornelius Cinna") and instead chose retirement.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadian200916-11) During Cinna's dominance, Caesar was named as _[flamen Dialis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamen\_Dialis "Flamen Dialis")_ (a priest of [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_(mythology) "Jupiter (mythology)")) which led to his marriage to Cinna's daughter, [Cornelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelia_(wife_of_Caesar) "Cornelia (wife of Caesar)"). The religious taboos of the priesthood would have forced Caesar to forgo a political career; the appointment – one of the highest non-political honours – indicates that there were few expectations of a major career for Caesar.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-12) In early 84 BC, Caesar's father died suddenly.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200634-13) After [Sulla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulla "Sulla")'s victory in the [civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulla's_civil_war "Sulla's civil war") (82 BC), Cinna's _acta_ were annulled. Sulla consequently ordered Caesar to abdicate and divorce Cinna's daughter. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment. Sulla may have put Caesar on the [proscription lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proscription_of_Sulla "Proscription of Sulla"), though scholars are mixed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-14) Caesar then went into hiding before his relatives and contacts among the [Vestal Virgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestal_Virgins "Vestal Virgins") were able to intercede on his behalf.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-15) They then reached a compromise where Caesar would resign his priesthood but keep his wife and chattels; Sulla's alleged remark he saw "in [Caesar] many [Mariuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Marius "Gaius Marius")"[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-16) is apocryphal.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-17)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Augustus_Bevilacqua_Glyptothek_Munich_317.jpg/250px-Augustus_Bevilacqua_Glyptothek_Munich_317.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Augustus_Bevilacqua_Glyptothek_Munich_317.jpg)

[Imperial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") bust of [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus") (known as the [Augustus Bevilacqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Bevilacqua?action=edit&redlink=1 "Augustus Bevilacqua (page does not exist)")) wearing the [civic crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_crown "Civic crown") ([Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _corona civica_). Caesar won the civic crown for his bravery at the [Siege of Mytilene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mytilene_(81_BC) "Siege of Mytilene (81 BC)") in 81 BC.

Caesar then left Italy to serve in the staff of the [governor of Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Roman_governors_of_Asia "List of Roman governors of Asia"), [Marcus Minucius Thermus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Minucius_Thermus "Marcus Minucius Thermus"). While there, he travelled to Bithynia to collect naval reinforcements and stayed some time as a guest of the king, [Nicomedes IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicomedes_IV "Nicomedes IV"), though [later invective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_of_Bithynia "Queen of Bithynia") connected Caesar to a homosexual relation with the monarch.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadian200917%E2%80%9318-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-19) He then served at the [Siege of Mytilene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mytilene_(81_BC) "Siege of Mytilene (81 BC)") where he won the [civic crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_crown "Civic crown") for saving the life of a fellow citizen in battle. The privileges of the crown – the Senate was supposed to stand on a holder's entrance and holders were permitted to wear the crown at public occasions – whetted Caesar's appetite for honours. After the capture of Mytilene, Caesar transferred to the staff of [Publius Servilius Vatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Servilius_Vatia_Isauricus "Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus") in Cilicia before learning of Sulla's death in 78 BC and returning home immediately.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadian200917-20) He was alleged to have wanted to join in on the consul [Lepidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aemilius_Lepidus_(consul_78_BC) "Marcus Aemilius Lepidus (consul 78 BC)")' revolt that year[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-21) but this is likely literary embellishment of Caesar's desire for [tyranny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyranny "Tyranny") from a young age.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202135-22)

Afterward, Caesar attacked some of the Sullan aristocracy in the courts but was unsuccessful in his attempted prosecution of [Gnaeus Cornelius Dolabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnaeus_Cornelius_Dolabella "Gnaeus Cornelius Dolabella") in 77 BC, who had recently returned from a proconsulship in [Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(Roman_province) "Macedonia (Roman province)"). Going after a less well-connected senator, he was successful the next year in prosecuting [Gaius Antonius Hybrida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Antonius_Hybrida "Gaius Antonius Hybrida") (later consul in 63 BC) for profiteering from the proscriptions but was forestalled when a tribune interceded on Antonius' behalf.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-23) After these oratorical attempts, Caesar left Rome for [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes "Rhodes") seeking the tutelage of the rhetorician [Apollonius Molon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollonius_Molon "Apollonius Molon").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadian200918-24) While travelling, he was intercepted and ransomed by pirates in a story that was later much embellished. According to Plutarch and Suetonius, he was freed after paying a ransom of fifty [talents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talent_(measurement) "Talent (measurement)") and responded by returning with a fleet to capture and execute the pirates. The recorded sum for the ransom is literary embellishment and it is more likely that the pirates were sold into slavery per [Velleius Paterculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velleius_Paterculus "Velleius Paterculus").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-25) His studies were interrupted by the outbreak of the [Third Mithridatic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Mithridatic_War "Third Mithridatic War") over the winter of 75 and 74 BC; Caesar is alleged to have gone around collecting troops in the province at the locals' expense and leading them successfully against Mithridates' forces.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-26)

### Entrance to politics

While absent from Rome, in 73 BC, Caesar was co-opted into the [pontifices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifices "Pontifices") in place of his deceased relative [Gaius Aurelius Cotta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Aurelius_Cotta "Gaius Aurelius Cotta"). The promotion marked him as a well-accepted member of the aristocracy with great future prospects in his political career.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200678-27) Caesar decided to return shortly thereafter and on his return was elected one of the [military tribunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_tribunes "Military tribunes") for 71 BC.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-28) There is no evidence that Caesar served in war – even though [the war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Servile_War "Third Servile War") on [Spartacus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spartacus "Spartacus") was ongoing – during his term; he did, however, agitate for the removal of Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for those who supported Lepidus' revolt to be pardoned.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-29) These advocacies were common and uncontroversial.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202163-30) The next year, 70 BC, [Pompey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey "Pompey") and [Crassus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crassus "Crassus") were consuls and brought legislation restoring the plebeian tribunate's rights; one of the tribunes, with Caesar supporting, then brought legislation pardoning the Lepidan exiles.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-31)

For his quaestorship in 69 BC, Caesar was allotted to serve under [Gaius Antistius Vetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Antistius_Vetus_(praetor_70_BC) "Gaius Antistius Vetus (praetor 70 BC)") in [Hispania Ulterior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania_Ulterior "Hispania Ulterior"). His election also gave him a lifetime seat in the Senate. However, before he left, his aunt Julia, the widow of Marius, died; and, soon afterwards, his wife Cornelia died shortly after bearing his only legitimate child, [Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(daughter_of_Caesar) "Julia (daughter of Caesar)"). He gave eulogies for both at public funerals.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-32) During his aunt's funeral, Caesar displayed the images of Marius, whose memory had been suppressed after Sulla's victory in the civil war. Some of the Sullan nobles – including [Quintus Lutatius Catulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Lutatius_Catulus_Capitolinus "Quintus Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus") – who had suffered under the Marian regime objected, but by this point depictions of husbands in aristocratic women's funerary processions was common.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202143-33) Contra Plutarch,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlut._''Caes.''5.2%E2%80%933-34) Caesar's action here was likely in keeping with a political trend for reconciliation and normalisation rather than a display of renewed factionalism.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202143%E2%80%9346-35) Caesar quickly remarried, taking the hand of Sulla's granddaughter [Pompeia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeia_(wife_of_Caesar) "Pompeia (wife of Caesar)").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-36)

### Aedileship and election as _pontifex maximus_

For much of this period, Caesar was one of [Pompey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey "Pompey")'s supporters. Caesar joined with Pompey in the late 70s to support restoration of tribunician rights; his support for the law recalling the Lepidan exiles may have been related to the same tribune's bill to grant lands to Pompey's veterans. Caesar also supported the _[lex Gabinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex\_Gabinia "Lex Gabinia")_ in 67 BC granting Pompey an extraordinary command against piracy in the Mediterranean and also supported the _[lex Manilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex\_Manilia "Lex Manilia")_ in 66 BC to reassign the Third Mithridatic War from its then-commander [Lucullus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucullus "Lucullus") to Pompey.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen199579%E2%80%9380-37)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Julius_Caesar_%26_C._Cossutius_Maridianus%2C_denarius%2C_44_BC%2C_RRC_480-19.jpg/330px-Julius_Caesar_%26_C._Cossutius_Maridianus%2C_denarius%2C_44_BC%2C_RRC_480-19.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Julius_Caesar_&_C._Cossutius_Maridianus,_denarius,_44_BC,_RRC_480-19.jpg)

Denarius of [C. Cossutius Maridianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Cossutius_Maridianus?action=edit&redlink=1 "C. Cossutius Maridianus (page does not exist)"), 44 BC, with the head of Julius Caesar as [pontifex maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifex_maximus "Pontifex maximus") on the obverse. The legend on the reverse mentions the [A. A. A. F. F.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triumvir_monetalis "Triumvir monetalis")

Four years after his aunt Julia's funeral, in 65 BC, Caesar served as [curule aedile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curule_aedile "Curule aedile") and staged lavish [games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludi "Ludi") that won him further attention and popular support.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-38) He also restored the trophies won by Marius, and taken down by Sulla, over [Jugurtha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugurthine_War "Jugurthine War") and the [Cimbri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cimbrian_War "Cimbrian War").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBroughton1952158-39) According to Plutarch's narrative, the trophies were restored overnight to the applause and tears of joy of the onlookers; however, any sudden and secret restoration of this sort would not have been possible – architects, restorers, and other workmen would have to have been hired and paid for – nor would it have been likely that the work could have been done in a single night.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202146%E2%80%9347-40) It is more likely that Caesar was merely restoring his family's public monuments – consistent with standard aristocratic practice and the virtue of _[pietas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietas "Pietas")_ – and, over objections from Catulus, these actions were broadly supported by the Senate.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202148%E2%80%9349-41)

In 63 BC, Caesar stood for the praetorship and also for the post of _[pontifex maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifex\_maximus "Pontifex maximus")_,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-42) who was the head of the [College of Pontiffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Pontiffs "College of Pontiffs") and the highest ranking state religious official. In the pontifical election before the [tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_tribe "Roman tribe"), Caesar faced two influential senators: [Quintus Lutatius Catulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Lutatius_Catulus_Capitolinus "Quintus Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus") and [Publius Servilius Isauricus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Servilius_Isauricus "Publius Servilius Isauricus"). Caesar came out victorious. Many scholars have expressed astonishment that Caesar's candidacy was taken seriously, but this was not without historical precedent.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-43) Ancient sources allege that Caesar paid huge bribes or was shamelessly ingratiating;[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-44) that no charge was ever laid alleging this implies that bribery alone is insufficient to explain his victory.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202167%E2%80%9368-45) If bribes or other monies were needed, they may have been underwritten by Pompey, whom Caesar at this time supported and who opposed Catulus' candidacy.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen199580%E2%80%9381-46)

Many sources also assert that Caesar supported the land reform proposals brought that year by plebeian tribune [Publius Servilius Rullus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Servilius_Rullus "Publius Servilius Rullus"), however, there are no ancient sources so attesting.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202169_n._148-47) Caesar also engaged in a collateral manner in the trial of [Gaius Rabirius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Rabirius_(senator) "Gaius Rabirius (senator)") by one of the plebeian tribunes – [Titus Labienus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titus_Labienus "Titus Labienus") – for the murder of Saturninus in accordance with a [senatus consultum ultimum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senatus_consultum_ultimum "Senatus consultum ultimum") some forty years earlier.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202171-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-49) The most famous event of the year was the [Catilinarian conspiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catilinarian_conspiracy "Catilinarian conspiracy"). While some of Caesar's enemies, including Catulus, alleged that he participated in the conspiracy,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-50) the chance that he was a participant is extremely small.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-51)

### Praetorship

Caesar won his election to the [praetorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praetorship "Praetorship") in 63 BC easily and, as one of the praetor-elects, spoke out that December in the Senate against executing certain citizens who had been arrested in the city conspiring with Gauls in furtherance of the conspiracy.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx202185%E2%80%9386,_90-52) Caesar's proposal at the time is not entirely clear. The earlier sources assert that he advocated life imprisonment without trial; the later sources assert he instead wanted the conspirators imprisoned pending trial. Most accounts agree that Caesar supported confiscation of the conspirators' property.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-53) Caesar likely advocated the former, which was a compromise position that would place the Senate within the bounds of the _lex Sempronia de capite civis_, and was initially successful in swaying the body; a later intervention by [Cato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cato_the_Younger "Cato the Younger"), however, swayed the Senate at the end for execution.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen1995281%E2%80%9382-54)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Cicero_Denounces_Catiline_in_the_Roman_Senate_by_Cesare_Maccari.png/500px-Cicero_Denounces_Catiline_in_the_Roman_Senate_by_Cesare_Maccari.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cicero_Denounces_Catiline_in_the_Roman_Senate_by_Cesare_Maccari.png)

[Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero "Cicero"), consul in 63 BC, depicted in an 1889 [fresco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresco "Fresco") denouncing Catiline and exposing his conspiracy before the Senate. When conspirators within the city were later arrested, Cicero referred their fate to the Senate, triggering a debate in which Caesar as praetor-elect participated.

During his year as praetor, Caesar first attempted to deprive his enemy Catulus of the honour of completing the rebuilt [Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Jupiter_Optimus_Maximus "Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus"), accusing him of embezzling funds, and threatening to bring legislation to reassign it to Pompey. This proposal was quickly dropped amid near-universal opposition.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021102-55) He then supported the attempt by plebeian tribune [Metellus Nepos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Caecilius_Metellus_Nepos_(consul_57_BC) "Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos (consul 57 BC)") to transfer the command against Catiline from the consul of 63, Gaius Antonius Hybrida, to Pompey. After a violent meeting of the [comitia tributa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comitia_tributa "Comitia tributa") in the forum, where Metellus came into fisticuffs with his tribunician colleagues Cato and [Quintus Minucius Thermus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Minucius_Thermus_(governor_of_Asia) "Quintus Minucius Thermus (governor of Asia)"),[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021102%E2%80%9304-56) the Senate passed a decree against Metellus – Suetonius claims that both Nepos and Caesar were deposed from their magistracies; this would have been a constitutional impossibility[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-57) – which led Caesar to distance himself from the proposals: hopes for a provincial command and need to repair relations with the aristocracy took priority.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021109-58) He also was engaged in the [Bona Dea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bona_Dea "Bona Dea") affair, where [Publius Clodius Pulcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Clodius_Pulcher "Publius Clodius Pulcher") sneaked into Caesar's house sacrilegiously during a female religious observance; Caesar avoided any part of the affair by divorcing his wife immediately – claiming that his wife needed to be "above suspicion"[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPlut._''Caes.''10.9-59) – but there is no indication that Caesar supported Clodius in any way.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-60)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Cato_Volubilis_bronze_bust.jpg/250px-Cato_Volubilis_bronze_bust.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cato_Volubilis_bronze_bust.jpg)

Bronze bust of Cato, Caesar's principal opponent in the Catilinarian debate and also a personal enemy. Cato may have been responsible for the law requiring declarations of candidacy in person within the _[pomerium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomerium "Pomerium")_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDrogula201997%E2%80%9398-61)

After his praetorship, Caesar was appointed to govern [Hispania Ulterior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispania_Ulterior "Hispania Ulterior")_pro consule_.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-62) Deeply indebted from his campaigns for the praetorship and for the pontificate, Caesar required military victory beyond the normal provincial extortion to pay them off.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021109%E2%80%9310-63) He campaigned against the [Callaeci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callaeci "Callaeci") and [Lusitani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusitani "Lusitani") and seized the Callaeci capital in northwestern Spain, bringing Roman troops to the Atlantic and seizing enough plunder to pay his debts.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBroughton1952180-64) Claiming to have completed the peninsula's conquest, he made for home after having been hailed _[imperator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperator "Imperator")_.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021110%E2%80%9311-65) When he arrived home in the summer of 60 BC, he was then forced to choose between a triumph and election to the consulship: either he could remain outside the _[pomerium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomerium "Pomerium")_ (Rome's sacred boundary) awaiting a triumph or cross the boundary, giving up his command and triumph, to make a declaration of consular candidacy.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021111-66) Attempts to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person were filibustered in the Senate by Caesar's enemy Cato, even though the Senate seemed to support the exception.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021112%E2%80%9313-67) Faced with the choice between a triumph and the consulship, Caesar chose the consulship.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-68)

## First consulship and the Gallic Wars

Main articles: [Military campaigns of Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_campaigns_of_Julius_Caesar "Military campaigns of Julius Caesar") and [First Triumvirate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Triumvirate "First Triumvirate")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/RSC_0022_-_transparent_background.png/330px-RSC_0022_-_transparent_background.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RSC_0022_-_transparent_background.png)

A [denarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denarius "Denarius") depicting Julius Caesar, dated to February–March 44 BC–the goddess [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_(mythology) "Venus (mythology)") is shown on the reverse, holding [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_(mythology) "Victoria (mythology)") and a sceptre. Caption: CAESAR IMP. M. / L. AEMILIVS BVCA.

Caesar stood for the consulship of 59 BC along with two other candidates. His political position at the time was strong: he had supporters among the families which had supported Marius or Cinna; his connection with the Sullan aristocracy was good; his support of Pompey had won him support in turn. His support for reconciliation in continuing aftershocks of the civil war was popular in all parts of society.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen200928-69) With the support of Crassus, who supported Caesar's joint ticket with one [Lucius Lucceius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Lucceius "Lucius Lucceius"), Caesar won. Lucceius, however, did not and the voters returned [Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Calpurnius_Bibulus "Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus") instead, one of Caesar's long-standing personal and political enemies.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen200930%E2%80%9331-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-71)

### First consulship

Further information: [First Triumvirate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Triumvirate "First Triumvirate")

After the elections, Caesar reconciled Pompey and Crassus, two political foes, in a three-way alliance misleadingly[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-72) termed the "First Triumvirate" in modern times.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-73) Caesar was still at work in December of 60 BC attempting to find allies for his consulship and the alliance was finalised only some time around its start.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen200931-74) Pompey and Crassus joined in pursuit of two respective goals: the ratification of [Pompey's eastern settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey's_eastern_settlement "Pompey's eastern settlement") and the bailing out of tax farmers in Asia, many of whom were Crassus' clients. All three sought the extended patronage of land grants, with Pompey especially seeking the promised land grants for his veterans.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-75)

Caesar's first act was to [publish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acta_Diurna "Acta Diurna") the minutes of the Senate and the assemblies, signalling the Senate's accountability to the public. He then brought in the Senate a bill – crafted to avoid objections to previous land reform proposals and any indications of radicalism – to purchase property from willing sellers to distribute to Pompey's veterans and the urban poor. It would be administered by a board of twenty (with Caesar excluded), and financed by Pompey's plunder and territorial gains.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen200932-76) Referring it to the Senate in hope that it would take up the matter to show its beneficence for the people,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021125%E2%80%9329-77) there was little opposition and the obstructionism that occurred was largely unprincipled, firmly opposing it not on grounds of public interest but rather opposition to Caesar's political advancement.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen200932-76) Unable to overcome Cato's filibustering, he moved the bill before the people and, at a public meeting, Caesar's co-consul Bibulus threatened a permanent veto for the entire year. This clearly violated the people's well-established legislative sovereignty[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021130,_132-78) and triggered a riot in which Bibulus' fasces were broken, symbolising popular rejection of his magistracy.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021138-79) The bill was then voted through. Bibulus attempted to induce the Senate to nullify it on grounds it was passed by violence and contrary to the auspices but the Senate refused.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021139%E2%80%9340-80)

Caesar also brought and passed a one-third write-down of tax farmers' arrears for Crassus and ratification of Pompey's eastern settlements. Both bills were passed with little or no debate in the Senate.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWiseman1994372-81) Caesar then moved to extend his agrarian bill to Campania some time in May; this may be when Bibulus withdrew to his house.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021143_(Bibulus),_147_(dating_to_May)-82) Pompey, shortly thereafter, also wed Caesar's daughter Julia to seal their alliance.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWiseman1994374-83) An ally of Caesar's, plebeian tribune [Publius Vatinius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Vatinius "Publius Vatinius") moved the _[lex Vatinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex\_Vatinia "Lex Vatinia")_ assigning the provinces of [Illyricum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illyricum_(Roman_province) "Illyricum (Roman province)") and [Cisalpine Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisalpine_Gaul "Cisalpine Gaul") to Caesar for five years.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDrogula2019137-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-85) Suetonius' claim that the Senate had assigned to Caesar the _silvae callesque_ ("woods and tracks") is likely an exaggeration: fear of Gallic invasion had grown in 60 BC and it is more likely that the consuls had been assigned to Italy, a defensive posture that Caesarian partisans dismissed as "mere 'forest tracks'".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-86) The Senate was also persuaded to assign to Caesar [Transalpine Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transalpine_Gaul "Transalpine Gaul") as well, subject to annual renewal, most likely to control his ability to make war on the far side of the Alps.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021176%E2%80%9377Gruen200934-87)

Some time in the year, perhaps after the passing of the bill distributing the Campanian land[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-88) and after these political defeats, Bibulus withdrew to his house. There, he issued edicts in absentia, purporting unprecedentedly to cancel all days on which Caesar or his allies could hold votes for religious reasons.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021142%E2%80%9344-89) Cato too attempted symbolic gestures against Caesar, which allowed him and his allies to "feign victimisation"; these tactics were successful in building revulsion to Caesar and his allies through the year.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-90)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-91) This opposition caused serious political difficulties to Caesar and his allies, belying the common depiction of triumviral political supremacy.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen200934-92) Later in the year, however, Caesar – with the support of his opponents – brought and passed the _[lex Julia de repetundis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex\_Julia\_de\_repetundis "Lex Julia de repetundis")_ to crack down on provincial corruption.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDrogula2019138%E2%80%9339,_noting_Cato's_support_of_Caesar's_anti-corruption_bill_and_the_possibility_that_Cato_gave_input_for_some_of_its_provisions-93) When his consulship ended, Caesar's legislation was challenged by two of the new praetors but discussion in the Senate stalled and was regardless dropped. He stayed near the city until some time around mid-March.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-94)

### Campaigns in Gaul

Main article: [Gallic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallic_Wars "Gallic Wars")

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Roman_republic%2C_territory_44_BC_labelled.svg/330px-Roman_republic%2C_territory_44_BC_labelled.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Roman_republic,_territory_44_BC_labelled.svg)

Extent of the Roman Republic in 44 BC after Caesar's conquests, with labels for the general area of provincial assignments.

During the Gallic Wars, Caesar wrote his _Commentaries_ thereon, which were acknowledged even in his time as a Latin literary masterwork. Meant to document Caesar's campaigns in his own words and maintain support in Rome for his military operations and career, he produced some ten volumes covering operations in Gaul from 58 to 52 BC.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006186%E2%80%9387-95) Each was likely produced in the year following the events described and was likely aimed at the general, or at least literate, population in Rome;[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006188%E2%80%9389-96) the account is naturally partial to Caesar – his defeats are excused and victories highlighted – but it is almost the sole source for events in Gaul in this period.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006189%E2%80%9390-97)

Gaul in 58 BC was in the midst of some instability. Tribes had raided into Transalpine Gaul and there was an on-going struggle between two tribes in central Gaul which collaterally involved Roman alliances and politics. The divisions within the Gauls – they were no unified bloc – would be exploited in the coming years.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006204-98) The first engagement was in April 58 BC when Caesar prevented the migrating [Helvetii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helvetii "Helvetii") from moving through Roman territory, allegedly because he feared they would unseat a Roman ally.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006205,_208%E2%80%9310-99) Building a wall, he stopped their movement near Geneva and – after raising two legions – defeated them at the [Battle of Bibracte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bibracte "Battle of Bibracte") before forcing them to return to their original homes.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2016212%E2%80%9315-100) He was drawn further north responding to requests from Gallic tribes, including the [Aedui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aedui "Aedui"), for aid against [Ariovistus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariovistus "Ariovistus") – king of the [Suebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suebi "Suebi") and a declared friend of Rome by the Senate during Caesar's own consulship – and he defeated them at the [Battle of Vosges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vosges_(58_BC) "Battle of Vosges (58 BC)").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2016217-101) Wintering in northeastern Gaul near the [Belgae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgae "Belgae") in the winter of 58–57, Caesar's forward military position triggered an uprising to remove his troops; able to eke out a victory at the [Battle of the Sabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Sabis "Battle of the Sabis"), Caesar spent much of 56 BC suppressing the Belgae and dispersing his troops to campaign across much of Gaul, including against the [Veneti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veneti_(Gaul) "Veneti (Gaul)") in what is now [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2016220-102) At this point, almost all of Gaul – except its central regions – fell under Roman subjugation.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoatwright2004242-103)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Lionel_Royer_-_Vercingetorix_Throwing_down_His_Weapons_at_the_feet_of_Julius_Caesar.jpg/330px-Lionel_Royer_-_Vercingetorix_Throwing_down_His_Weapons_at_the_feet_of_Julius_Caesar.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lionel_Royer_-_Vercingetorix_Throwing_down_His_Weapons_at_the_feet_of_Julius_Caesar.jpg)

[Vercingetorix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vercingetorix "Vercingetorix") throws down his arms at the feet of Julius Caesar, painting by [Lionel Royer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Royer "Lionel Royer") in 1899. [Musée Crozatier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_Crozatier "Musée Crozatier"), [Le Puy-en-Velay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Puy-en-Velay "Le Puy-en-Velay"), France.

Seeking to buttress his military reputation, he engaged Germans attempting to cross the Rhine, which marked it as a Roman frontier;[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoatwright2004242-103) he here built a [bridge across the Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar's_Rhine_bridges "Caesar's Rhine bridges") in a feat of engineering meant to show Rome's ability to project power.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2016203-104) Ostensibly seeking to interdict British aid to his Gallic enemies, he led expeditions into southern Britain in 55 and 54 BC, perhaps seeking further conquests or otherwise wanting to impress readers in Rome; Britain at the time was to the Romans an "island of mystery" and "a land of wonder".[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2016221%E2%80%9322Boatwright2004242-105) He, however, withdrew from the island in the face of winter uprisings in Gaul led by the [Eburones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eburones "Eburones") and [Belgae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgae "Belgae") starting in late 54 BC which ambushed and virtually annihilated a legion and five cohorts.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2016222-106) Caesar was, however, able to lure the rebels into unfavourable terrain and routed them in battle.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2016223-107) The next year, a greater challenge emerged with the uprising of most of central Gaul, led by [Vercingetorix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vercingetorix "Vercingetorix") of the [Averni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Averni "Averni"). Caesar was initially defeated at [Gergovia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gergovia "Battle of Gergovia") before [besieging Vercingetorix at Alesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Alesia "Battle of Alesia"). After becoming himself besieged, Caesar won a major victory which forced Vercingetorix's surrender; Caesar then spent much of his time into 51 BC suppressing any remaining resistance.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2016229%E2%80%9332,_233%E2%80%9338Boatwright2004242-108)

### Politics, Gaul, and Rome

In the initial years from the end of Caesar's consulship in 59 BC, the three so-called triumvirs sought to maintain the goodwill of the extremely popular [Publius Clodius Pulcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Clodius_Pulcher "Publius Clodius Pulcher"),[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-109) who was [plebeian tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plebeian_tribune "Plebeian tribune") in 58 BC and in that year successfully sent Cicero into exile. When Clodius took an anti-Pompeian stance later that year, he unsettled Pompey's eastern arrangements, started attacking the validity of Caesar's consular legislation, and by August 58 forced Pompey into seclusion. Caesar and Pompey responded by successfully backing the election of magistrates to recall Cicero from exile on the condition that Cicero would refrain from criticism or obstruction of the allies.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamsey200937%E2%80%9338-110)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamsey200939-112)

Politics in Rome fell into violent street clashes between Clodius and two tribunes who were friends of Cicero. With Cicero now supporting Caesar and Pompey, Caesar sent news of Gaul to Rome and claimed total victory and [pacification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacification_(military_action) "Pacification (military action)"). The Senate at Cicero's motion voted him an unprecedented fifteen days of thanksgiving.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-113) Such reports were necessary for Caesar, especially in light of senatorial opponents, to prevent the Senate from reassigning his command in Transalpine Gaul, even if his position in Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum was guaranteed by the _lex Vatinia_ until 54 BC.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021196,_220Ramsey200939%E2%80%9340-114) His success was evidently recognised when the Senate voted state funds for some of Caesar's legions, which until this time Caesar had paid for personally.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021220%E2%80%9321-115)

The three allies' relations broke down in 57 BC: one of Pompey's allies challenged Caesar's land reform bill and the allies had a poor showing in the elections that year.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamsey200939%E2%80%9340-116) With a real threat to Caesar's command and _acta_ brewing in 56 BC under the aegis of the unfriendly consuls, Caesar needed his allies' political support.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021229-117) Pompey and Crassus too wanted military commands. Their combined interests led to a renewal of the alliance; drawing in the support of [Appius Claudius Pulcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appius_Claudius_Pulcher_(consul_54_BC) "Appius Claudius Pulcher (consul 54 BC)") and his younger brother Clodius for the consulship of 54 BC, they planned second consulships with following governorships in 55 BC for both Pompey and Crassus. Caesar, for his part, would receive a five-year extension of command.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamsey200941%E2%80%9342Morstein-Marx2021232-118)

Cicero was induced to oppose reassignment of Caesar's provinces and to defend a number of the allies' clients; his gloomy predictions of a triumviral set of consuls-designate for years on end proved an exaggeration when, only by desperate tactics, bribery, intimidation and violence were Pompey and Crassus elected consuls for 55 BC.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamsey200943Morstein-Marx2021232%E2%80%9333-119) During their consulship, Pompey and Crassus passed – with some tribunician support – the _lex Pompeia Licinia_ extending Caesar's command and the [_lex Trebonia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Trebonia_(55_BC) "Lex Trebonia (55 BC)") giving them respective commands in Spain and Syria,[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamsey200944Morstein-Marx2021232%E2%80%9333-120) though Pompey never left for the province and remained politically active at Rome.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGruen1995451-121) The opposition again unified against their heavy-handed political tactics – though not against Caesar's activities in Gaul[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-122) – and defeated the allies in the elections of that year.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamsey200944-123)

The ambush and destruction in Gaul of a legion and five cohorts in the winter of 55–54 BC produced substantial concern in Rome about Caesar's command and competence, evidenced by the highly defensive narrative in Caesar's _Commentaries_.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-124) The death of Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife Julia in childbirth c.late August 54 did not create a rift between Caesar and Pompey.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-126)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-127) At the start of 53 BC, Caesar sought and received reinforcements by recruitment and a private deal with Pompey before two years of largely unsuccessful campaigning against Gallic insurgents.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021243%E2%80%9344-128) In the same year, Crassus's campaign ended in disaster at the [Battle of Carrhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Carrhae "Battle of Carrhae"), culminating in his death at the hands of the [Parthians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthian_Empire "Parthian Empire"). When in 52 BC Pompey started the year with a sole consulship to restore order to the city,[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-129) Caesar was in Gaul suppressing insurgencies; after news of his victory at Alesia, with the support of Pompey he received twenty days of thanksgiving and, pursuant to the "Law of the Ten Tribunes", the right to stand for the consulship in absentia.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021247%E2%80%9348,_260,_265%E2%80%9366-130)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWiseman1994412-131)

## Civil war

Main article: [Caesar's civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar's_civil_war "Caesar's civil war")

Further information: [Alexandrine war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandrine_war "Alexandrine war"), [Early life of Cleopatra VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_life_of_Cleopatra_VII "Early life of Cleopatra VII"), and [Reign of Cleopatra VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Cleopatra_VII "Reign of Cleopatra VII")

A Roman bust of [Pompey the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey_the_Great "Pompey the Great") made during the reign of [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus") (27 BC–14 AD), a copy of an original bust from 70 to 60 BC, [Venice National Archaeological Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_National_Archaeological_Museum "Venice National Archaeological Museum"), Italy

From the period 52 to 49 BC, trust between Caesar and Pompey disintegrated.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021258-132) In 51 BC, the consul [Marcellus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Claudius_Marcellus_(consul_51_BC) "Marcus Claudius Marcellus (consul 51 BC)") proposed recalling Caesar, arguing that his _provincia_ (here meaning "task") in Gaul – due to his victory against Vercingetorix in 52 – was complete; it evidently was incomplete as Caesar was that year fighting the [Bellovaci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellovaci "Bellovaci")[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-133) and regardless the proposal was vetoed.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021270Drogula2019223-134) That year, it seemed that the conservatives around Cato in the Senate would seek to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honours or a second consulship.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021273-135) Cato, Bibulus, and their allies, however, were successful in winning Pompey over to take a hard line against Caesar's continued command.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021272,_276,_295_(identities_of_Cato's_allies)-136)

As 50 BC progressed, fears of civil war grew; both Caesar and his opponents started building up troops in southern Gaul and [northern Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Italy "Northern Italy"), respectively.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021291-137) In the autumn, Cicero and others sought disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, and on 1 December 50 BC this was formally proposed in the Senate.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021292%E2%80%9393-138) It received overwhelming support – 370 to 22 – but was not passed when [one of the consuls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Claudius_Marcellus_(consul_50_BC) "Gaius Claudius Marcellus (consul 50 BC)") dissolved the meeting.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021297-139) That year, when a rumour came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepted as a last resort.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-140) At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was read to the Senate and was rejected by the hardliners.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021304-141) A later compromise given privately to Pompey was also rejected at their insistence.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021306-142) On 7 January, his supportive tribunes were driven from Rome; the Senate then declared Caesar an enemy and it issued its _[senatus consultum ultimum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senatus\_consultum\_ultimum "Senatus consultum ultimum")_.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021308-143)

There is scholarly disagreement as to the specific reasons why Caesar marched on Rome. A very popular theory is that Caesar was forced to choose – when denied the immunity of his proconsular tenure – between prosecution, conviction, and exile, or civil war in defence of his position.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoatwright2004247Meier19951,_4Mackay2009279%E2%80%9381Wiseman1994419-144)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEhrhardt199530._%22Everyone_knows_that_Caesar_crossed_the_Rubicon_because_[he_would_have_been...]_put_on_trial,_found_guilty_and_have_his_political_career_ended..._Yet_over_thirty_years_ago,_Shackleton_Bailey,_in_less_than_two_pages_of_his_introduction_to_Cicero's_''Letters_to_Atticus'',_destroyed_the_basis_for_this_belief,_and..._no_one_has_been_able_to_rebuild_it%22-145) Whether Caesar actually would have been prosecuted and convicted is debated. Some scholars believe the possibility of successful prosecution was extremely unlikely.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-146)[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-147) Caesar's main objectives were to secure a second consulship – first mooted in 52 as colleague to Pompey's sole consulship[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-148) – and a triumph. He feared that his opponents – then holding both consulships for 50 BC – would reject his candidacy or refuse to ratify an election he won.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-149) This also was the core of his war justification: that Pompey and his allies were planning, by force if necessary (indicated in the expulsion of the tribunes[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021309-150)), to suppress the liberty of the Roman people to elect Caesar and honour his accomplishments.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorstein-Marx2021320-151)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Peach and ice cream dessert

For the Melba Moore album, see [Peach Melba (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba_(album) "Peach Melba (album)").

Peach Melba[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Peach_Melba.jpg/250px-Peach_Melba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peach_Melba.jpg)
Type[Dessert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dessert "Dessert")
Created by[Auguste Escoffier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Escoffier "Auguste Escoffier")
Main ingredients[Peaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach "Peach"), [raspberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raspberry "Raspberry") sauce, [vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla "Vanilla") ice cream
*   [![Image 5: Wikimedia Commons logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/4a/Commons-logo.svg/20px-Commons-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commons-logo.svg)[Media: Peach Melba](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Peach%20Melba "commons:Category:Peach Melba")

**Peach Melba** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _pêche Melba_, pronounced[[pɛʃ mɛlba]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")) is a dessert of [peaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach "Peach") and [raspberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raspberry "Raspberry") sauce with [vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla "Vanilla") ice cream. It was invented in 1892 or 1893 by the French chef [Auguste Escoffier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Escoffier "Auguste Escoffier") at the [Savoy Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Hotel "Savoy Hotel"), London, to honour the Australian [soprano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano "Soprano")[Nellie Melba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nellie_Melba "Nellie Melba").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-larousse-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Avey-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peach_Melba&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1892, operatic soprano Nellie Melba was performing in Wagner's opera _[Lohengrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lohengrin\_(opera) "Lohengrin (opera)")_ at [Covent Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Opera_House "Royal Opera House"). The [Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Philippe,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Prince Philippe, Duke of Orléans") gave a dinner party at the Savoy to celebrate her triumph. For the occasion, [Escoffier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Escoffier "Auguste Escoffier") presented Nellie with a dessert of fresh peaches served over vanilla ice cream in a silver dish perched atop an [ice sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_sculpture "Ice sculpture") of a swan, which is featured in the opera. He originally called the dish _Pêche au cygne_, or "peach with a swan."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Avey-2)

A few years later Escoffier created a new version of the dessert: when Escoffier and [César Ritz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Ritz "César Ritz") opened the [Ritz Carlton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlton_Hotel,_London "Carlton Hotel, London") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") (after both were sacked from the Savoy for alleged larceny, embezzlement, and fraud),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Levy-3) Escoffier changed the recipe slightly by adding a topping of sweetened raspberry purée and renamed the dish _Pêche Melba_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Avey-2)

## Variations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peach_Melba&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Variations")]

Other versions substitute pears, apricots, or strawberries instead of peaches or use raspberry sauce or melted redcurrant jelly instead of raspberry purée.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-larousse-1) The original dessert used simple ingredients of "tender and very ripe peaches, vanilla ice cream, and a purée of sugared raspberry". Escoffier himself is quoted as saying, "Any variation on this recipe ruins the delicate balance of its taste."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Avey-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-4)

### _Pijama_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peach_Melba&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Pijama")]

Peach Melba is claimed to be the ancestor of the _pijama_, a dessert in [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalonia "Catalonia") cuisine. 7 Portes, a famous restaurant in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona") founded in 1836, is credited with its creation in 1951, when officers of the U.S. [Sixth Fleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Fleet "Sixth Fleet") stationed in the nearby harbor would often dine at 7 Portes and order peach Melba for dessert. The name mutated to _pijama_ ([[pi.ˈʒa.mə]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Catalan "Help:IPA/Catalan"), [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_language "Catalan language") for _pajamas_) among the Catalan-speaking kitchen staff. From there the recipe, or the essence of it, spread throughout Catalonia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-5) Variations are countless, but ice cream, [flan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A8me_caramel "Crème caramel"), and fruit in syrup (peach or [pineapple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pineapple "Pineapple")) are its staple ingredients.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-catalunyacuina-6)

Though regarded as an extravagant and somewhat outdated dish today, the pijama was considered part of the corpus of the [Catalan cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_cuisine "Catalan cuisine") and its recipe was included in the inventory published by the Foundation of the Catalan Institute of Cuisine and Gastronomical Culture.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-catalunyacuina-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-7)

## Cultural significance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peach_Melba&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cultural significance")]

In tribute to Escoffier an elaborate deconstruction of the peach Melba was served as the last dish at [El Bulli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bulli "El Bulli") prior to its closure in 2012.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Peach and ice cream dessert

For the Melba Moore album, see [Peach Melba (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba_(album) "Peach Melba (album)").

Peach Melba[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Peach_Melba.jpg/250px-Peach_Melba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peach_Melba.jpg)
Type[Dessert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dessert "Dessert")
Created by[Auguste Escoffier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Escoffier "Auguste Escoffier")
Main ingredients[Peaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach "Peach"), [raspberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raspberry "Raspberry") sauce, [vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla "Vanilla") ice cream
*   [![Image 5: Wikimedia Commons logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/4a/Commons-logo.svg/20px-Commons-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commons-logo.svg)[Media: Peach Melba](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Peach%20Melba "commons:Category:Peach Melba")

**Peach Melba** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _pêche Melba_, pronounced[[pɛʃ mɛlba]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")) is a dessert of [peaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach "Peach") and [raspberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raspberry "Raspberry") sauce with [vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla "Vanilla") ice cream. It was invented in 1892 or 1893 by the French chef [Auguste Escoffier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Escoffier "Auguste Escoffier") at the [Savoy Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Hotel "Savoy Hotel"), London, to honour the Australian [soprano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano "Soprano")[Nellie Melba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nellie_Melba "Nellie Melba").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-larousse-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Avey-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peach_Melba&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1892, operatic soprano Nellie Melba was performing in Wagner's opera _[Lohengrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lohengrin\_(opera) "Lohengrin (opera)")_ at [Covent Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Opera_House "Royal Opera House"). The [Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Philippe,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Prince Philippe, Duke of Orléans") gave a dinner party at the Savoy to celebrate her triumph. For the occasion, [Escoffier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Escoffier "Auguste Escoffier") presented Nellie with a dessert of fresh peaches served over vanilla ice cream in a silver dish perched atop an [ice sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_sculpture "Ice sculpture") of a swan, which is featured in the opera. He originally called the dish _Pêche au cygne_, or "peach with a swan."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Avey-2)

A few years later Escoffier created a new version of the dessert: when Escoffier and [César Ritz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Ritz "César Ritz") opened the [Ritz Carlton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlton_Hotel,_London "Carlton Hotel, London") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") (after both were sacked from the Savoy for alleged larceny, embezzlement, and fraud),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Levy-3) Escoffier changed the recipe slightly by adding a topping of sweetened raspberry purée and renamed the dish _Pêche Melba_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Avey-2)

## Variations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peach_Melba&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Variations")]

Other versions substitute pears, apricots, or strawberries instead of peaches or use raspberry sauce or melted redcurrant jelly instead of raspberry purée.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-larousse-1) The original dessert used simple ingredients of "tender and very ripe peaches, vanilla ice cream, and a purée of sugared raspberry". Escoffier himself is quoted as saying, "Any variation on this recipe ruins the delicate balance of its taste."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-Avey-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-4)

### _Pijama_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peach_Melba&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Pijama")]

Peach Melba is claimed to be the ancestor of the _pijama_, a dessert in [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalonia "Catalonia") cuisine. 7 Portes, a famous restaurant in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona") founded in 1836, is credited with its creation in 1951, when officers of the U.S. [Sixth Fleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Fleet "Sixth Fleet") stationed in the nearby harbor would often dine at 7 Portes and order peach Melba for dessert. The name mutated to _pijama_ ([[pi.ˈʒa.mə]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Catalan "Help:IPA/Catalan"), [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_language "Catalan language") for _pajamas_) among the Catalan-speaking kitchen staff. From there the recipe, or the essence of it, spread throughout Catalonia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-5) Variations are countless, but ice cream, [flan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A8me_caramel "Crème caramel"), and fruit in syrup (peach or [pineapple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pineapple "Pineapple")) are its staple ingredients.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-catalunyacuina-6)

Though regarded as an extravagant and somewhat outdated dish today, the pijama was considered part of the corpus of the [Catalan cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_cuisine "Catalan cuisine") and its recipe was included in the inventory published by the Foundation of the Catalan Institute of Cuisine and Gastronomical Culture.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-catalunyacuina-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-7)

## Cultural significance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peach_Melba&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cultural significance")]

In tribute to Escoffier an elaborate deconstruction of the peach Melba was served as the last dish at [El Bulli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Bulli "El Bulli") prior to its closure in 2012.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peach_Melba#cite_note-9)
