Writing about RPF intimidation of opposition candidates in the run-up to elections, Caplan said "what was most infuriating was that none of this was necessary for the RPF to hold on to power". Belgian academic [Filip Reyntjens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filip_Reyntjens "Filip Reyntjens") disagrees, however, stating that "the RPF is fully aware that opening up the political system would eventually lead to a loss of power".[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReyntjens2011-178)

#### Presidential election, 2003

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Presidential election, 2003")]

Main article: [2003 Rwandan presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Rwandan_presidential_election "2003 Rwandan presidential election")

The first post-genocide election was held in August 2003, following the adoption of the new constitution.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(VIII)2003-179) In May, the parliament voted to ban the [Republican Democratic Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Democratic_Movement "Republican Democratic Movement") (MDR), following a parliamentary commission report accusing the MDR of "divisive" ideology.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIRIN_(II)2003-180) The MDR had been one of the coalition parties in the transitional government of national unity, and was the second-largest party in the country after the RPF.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(IX)2003-181)[Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") criticised this move, claiming that "the unfounded allegations against the individuals mentioned in the report appear to be part of a government-orchestrated crackdown on the political opposition".[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmnesty_International_(I)2003-182) Kagame was the RPF candidate, while former prime minister Twagiramungu was his main challenger. Twagiramungu had intended to run as the candidate for the MDR, but instead sought the presidency as an independent following the party's banishment.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIRIN_(III)2003-183) He returned to the country from Europe in June 2003 and began campaigning in August.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIRIN_(III)2003-183)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(X)2003-184)

Kagame declared victory in the election one day after the poll,[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeaver_County_Times2003-185) and his win was later confirmed by the National Electoral Commission.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTENunley-186) The final results showed that Kagame received 95.1 per cent of the vote, Twagiramungu 3.6 per cent, and the third candidate, Jean Nepomuscene Nayinzira, 1.3 per cent; the voter turnout was 96.6 per cent.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTENunley-186) The campaign, election day, and aftermath were largely peaceful, although an observer from the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU) raised concerns about intimidation of opposition supporters by the RPF.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReuters_(I)2003-187) Twagiramungu rejected the result of the election and also questioned the margin of victory, saying "Almost 100 per cent? That's not possible".[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReuters_(I)2003-187) He filed a petition at the Supreme Court to nullify the result, but was unsuccessful and he left Rwanda shortly afterwards, fearing that he would be arrested.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIRIN_(IV)2003-188)[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEImmigration_and_Refugee_Board_of_Canada2006-189) The EU observer also questioned the result, citing "numerous irregularities", but also describing the poll as a "positive step" in the country's history.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECPJ2004-190)

#### Presidential election, 2010

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Presidential election, 2010")]

Main article: [2010 Rwandan presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Rwandan_presidential_election "2010 Rwandan presidential election")

[![Image 13: Close up photo of Paul Kagame smiling at the premiere of the film Earth Made of Glass](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Paul_Kagame_New_York_2010.jpg/250px-Paul_Kagame_New_York_2010.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Kagame_New_York_2010.jpg)

Kagame in 2010

Kagame ran for re-election in 2010, at the end of his first elected term.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECJCR2003articles_100%E2%80%93101-191)[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoss2010-192) He was endorsed by the RPF national congress as their candidate in May 2010, and was accepted as a candidate in July.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKagireStraziuso2010-193) His highest-profile opponent was [Victoire Ingabire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoire_Ingabire "Victoire Ingabire"), a Hutu who had been living abroad for some years, and returned to Rwanda in January 2010 to run for the presidency.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKagireStraziuso2010-193) After a series of criticisms of Kagame's policies, she was arrested in April and prohibited from running in the election,[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhewell2010-194)[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTENew_Times_(I)2010-195) as part of what Amnesty International's Tawanda Hondora described as "pre-electoral repression".[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-196) Kagame began his campaign with a rally at Kigali's [Amahoro Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amahoro_Stadium "Amahoro Stadium") on 20 July,[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-197) and held rallies across the country during the subsequent campaign period.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBraquehaisNorris-Trent2010-198) The rallies attracted tens of thousands, shouting enthusiastically for Kagame, although reporters for _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ interviewed a number of Rwandans who said that they were "not free to vote against him and that government officials down to the village level had put enormous pressure on them to register to vote; contribute some of their meager earnings to Mr. Kagame's campaign; and attend rallies".[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGettlemanKron2010-199)

The election went ahead in August 2010 without Ingabire and two other banned candidates, Kagame facing three opponents described by Human Rights Watch as "broadly supportive of the RPF".[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuman_Rights_Watch_(II)2010-200) Kagame went on to receive 93.08 per cent of the vote in the election. Opposition and human rights groups said that the election was tainted by repression, murder, and lack of credible competition. Kagame responded by saying "I see no problems, but there are some people who choose to see problems where there are not."[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAl_Jazeera_(II)2010-201)

#### Constitutional referendum, 2015

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Constitutional referendum, 2015")]

Main article: [2015 Rwandan constitutional referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Rwandan_constitutional_referendum "2015 Rwandan constitutional referendum")

As Kagame's second term progressed, he began to hint that he might seek to rewrite the term-limit clause of the Rwandan constitution, to allow him to run for a third term in the 2017 elections.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2014-202) Earlier in his presidency he had ruled it out,[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2014-202) but in a 2014 speech at [Tufts University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tufts_University "Tufts University") in the United States, Kagame said that he did not know when he would leave office, and that it was up to the Rwandan people to decide.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2014-202) He told delegates "...let's wait and see what happens as we go. Whatever will happen, we'll have an explanation."[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2014-202) The following year, a protest occurred outside [parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Rwanda "Parliament of Rwanda"),[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaing2015-203) and a petition signed by 3.7 million people—more than half of the electorate—was presented to lawmakers asking for Kagame to be allowed to stay in office.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgence_France-Presse2015-204) The parliament responded by passing an amendment to the constitution in November 2015, with both the [Chamber of Deputies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_of_Deputies_of_Rwanda "Chamber of Deputies of Rwanda") and the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Rwanda "Senate of Rwanda") voting unanimously in favour.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAl_Jazeera_(IV)2015-205) The motion passed kept the two-term limit in place, and also reduced the length of terms from 7 years to 5 years, but it made an explicit exception for Kagame, who would be permitted to run for a third 7-year term followed by two further 5-year terms, if he so desired.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAl_Jazeera_(IV)2015-205) After the amendment was passed in parliament, a referendum was required for it to come into effect.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAl_Jazeera_(IV)2015-205)

The referendum took place on 18 December 2015, with Rwandans overseas voting on 17 December.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(XVIII)2015-206) The amendment was approved by the electorate, with 6.16 million voters saying yes, approximately 98 per cent of the votes.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcVeigh2015-171) The electoral commission stated that the vote had been peaceful and orderly.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcVeigh2015-171) The [Democratic Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Green_Party_of_Rwanda "Democratic Green Party of Rwanda"), the most prominent domestic group opposing the change, protested that it had not been permitted to campaign openly against the amendment.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcVeigh2015-171) Human Rights Watch executive director [Ken Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Roth "Ken Roth") announced on [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") that he did not believe the election to be free and fair, saying there was "no suspense in Rwanda referendum when so many dissidents silenced, civil society stifled".[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcVeigh2015-171) The amendment itself was criticised by the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") and also the United States, which released a statement saying that Kagame should respect the previous term limits and "foster a new generation of leaders in Rwanda".[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcVeigh2015-171) Kagame responded that it was not his own decision to seek a third term, but that the parliament and the people had demanded it.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcVeigh2015-171)

**Paul Kagame**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-1) (born 23 October 1957) is a Rwandan politician and former military officer who has been the president of Rwanda since 2000. He was previously considered Rwanda's _[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_facto "De facto")_ leader between 1994 and 2000, while [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_Rwanda "Vice President of Rwanda") and [Minister of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Defense_(Rwanda) "Minister of Defense (Rwanda)") under President [Pasteur Bizimungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteur_Bizimungu "Pasteur Bizimungu"), until assuming the Presidency in 2000. He was previously a commander of the [Rwandan Patriotic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Patriotic_Front "Rwandan Patriotic Front") (RPF), a rebel armed force which invaded [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda") in 1990. The RPF was one of the main belligerents of the [Rwandan Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Civil_War "Rwandan Civil War") and was the armed force which ended the 1994 [Rwandan genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide").

Born to a [Tutsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutsi "Tutsi") family in southern Rwanda that fled to [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") when he was two years old, Kagame spent the rest of his childhood there during the [Rwandan Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Revolution "Rwandan Revolution"), which ended Tutsi political dominance. In the 1980s, Kagame fought in [Yoweri Museveni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoweri_Museveni "Yoweri Museveni")'s rebel army becoming a senior Ugandan army officer after many military victories led Museveni to the [Ugandan presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Uganda "President of Uganda"). Kagame joined the RPF, taking control of the group when previous leader [Fred Rwigyema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Rwigyema "Fred Rwigyema") died on the second day of the 1990 invasion. By 1993, the RPF controlled significant territory in Rwanda and [a ceasefire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arusha_Accords_(Rwanda) "Arusha Accords (Rwanda)") was negotiated. The [assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Juv%C3%A9nal_Habyarimana_and_Cyprien_Ntaryamira "Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira") of Rwandan president [Juvénal Habyarimana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juv%C3%A9nal_Habyarimana "Juvénal Habyarimana") set off the [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide"), in which [Hutu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutu "Hutu") extremists killed an estimated 500,000 to 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu. Kagame resumed the civil war and ended the genocide with a military victory.

During his vice presidency, Kagame controlled the national army and was responsible for maintaining the government's power, while other officials began rebuilding the country. Many RPF soldiers carried out retribution killings. Kagame said he did not support these killings but failed to stop them. Hutu refugee camps formed in [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire") and other countries and the RPF attacked the camps in 1996, but insurgents continued to attack Rwanda. As part of the invasion, Kagame sponsored two rebel wars in Zaire. Rwandan- and Ugandan-backed rebels won the [first war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Congo_War "First Congo War") (1996–97), installing [Laurent-Désiré Kabila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent-D%C3%A9sir%C3%A9_Kabila "Laurent-Désiré Kabila") as [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_heads_of_state_of_the_Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "List of heads of state of the Democratic Republic of the Congo") in place of dictator [Mobutu Sese Seko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobutu_Sese_Seko "Mobutu Sese Seko") and returning Zaire to its former pre-Mobutu name, the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo") (DRC). The [second war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Congo_War "Second Congo War") was launched in 1998 against Kabila, and later his son [Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Kabila "Joseph Kabila"), following the DRC government's expulsion of Rwandan and Ugandan military forces from the country. The war escalated into a conflict that lasted until a 2003 peace deal and ceasefire.

Bizimungu resigned in 2000, most likely having been forced to do so, following a falling out with the RPF. He was replaced by Kagame. Bizimungu was later imprisoned for corruption and inciting ethnic violence, charges that human rights groups described as politically motivated. Kagame's rule is considered authoritarian, and human rights groups accuse him of political repression. Overall opinion on the regime by foreign observers is mixed, and as president, Kagame has prioritised national development, launching programmes which have led to development on key indicators including [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Rwanda "Healthcare in Rwanda"), [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Rwanda "Education in Rwanda") and [economic growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Rwanda "Economy of Rwanda"). Kagame has had mostly good relations with the [East African Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Community "East African Community") and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda%E2%80%93United_States_relations "Rwanda–United States relations"); his relations with France were poor until 2009. Relations with the DRC remain tense despite the 2003 ceasefire; human rights groups and a leaked United Nations report allege Rwandan support for two insurgencies in the country, a charge Kagame denies. Several countries suspended aid payments in 2012 following these allegations. Since coming to power, Kagame has won [four presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Rwanda "Elections in Rwanda"), but none of these have been rated free or fair by international observers. His role in the assassination of exiled political opponents has been controversial.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Kagame was born on 23 October 1957, the youngest of six children,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh20048-2) in Tambwe, [Ruanda-Urundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruanda-Urundi "Ruanda-Urundi"), a village located in what is now the [Southern Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Province,_Rwanda "Southern Province, Rwanda") of Rwanda.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOffice_of_the_President_(I)2011-3) His father, Deogratias Rutagambwa, was a member of the [Tutsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutsi "Tutsi") ethnic group, from which the royal family had been derived since the 18th century or earlier.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChr%C3%A9tien2003160-4) A member of the Bega clan, Deogratias Rutagambwa had family ties to King [Mutara III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutara_III_of_Rwanda "Mutara III of Rwanda"), but he pursued an independent business career rather than maintain a close connection to the royal court.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh20048-2) However, Rutagambwa's uncle [Rwubusisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwubusisi "Rwubusisi") was a powerful and influential politician.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTESingiza-5) Kagame's mother, Asteria Bisinda, descended from the family of the last Rwandan queen, [Rosalie Gicanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalie_Gicanda "Rosalie Gicanda"), that is from the Hebera branch of the royal Nyiginya clan.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDelmas1950-6)

At the time of Kagame's birth, Rwanda was a [United Nations Trust Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Trust_Territories "United Nations Trust Territories") which had been ruled, in various forms, by [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_colonial_empire "Belgian colonial empire") since 1916 under a mandate to oversee eventual [independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonization_of_Africa "Decolonization of Africa").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnited_Nations_(II)-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnited_Nations_(III)-8) Rwandans were made up of three distinct groups: the minority Tutsi were the traditional ruling class, and the Belgian colonial administration had long promoted Tutsi supremacy,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAppiahGates2010450-9) while the majority [Hutu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutu "Hutu") were agriculturalists.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier199911%E2%80%9312-10) The third group, the [Twa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twa "Twa"), were a forest-dwelling [pygmy people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmy_peoples "Pygmy peoples") descended from Rwanda's earliest inhabitants, who formed less than 1% of the population.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMamdani200261-11)

Tensions between Tutsi and Hutu had been escalating during the 1950s, and culminated in the 1959 [Rwandan Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Revolution "Rwandan Revolution"). Hutu activists began killing Tutsi, forcing more than 100,000 Tutsis to seek refuge in neighbouring countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGourevitch200058%E2%80%9359-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier199951-13) Kagame's family abandoned their home and lived for two years in northeastern Rwanda, eventually crossing the border into [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda"). They moved gradually north, and settled in the Nshungerezi refugee camp in the [Toro sub-region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toro_sub-region "Toro sub-region") in 1962.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh20048-2) It was around this time that Kagame first met [Fred Rwigyema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Rwigyema "Fred Rwigyema"), the future leader of the [Rwandan Patriotic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Patriotic_Front "Rwandan Patriotic Front").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200812-14)

Kagame began his primary education in a school near the refugee camp, where he and other Rwandan refugees learned how to speak English and began to integrate into Ugandan culture.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh200410-15) At the age of nine, he moved to the respected Rwengoro Primary School, around 16 kilometres (10 mi) away.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200813-16) He subsequently attended [Ntare School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ntare_School "Ntare School"), one of the best schools in Uganda, which was also the alma mater of future Ugandan President [Yoweri Museveni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoweri_Museveni "Yoweri Museveni").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200813-16) According to Kagame, the death of his father in the early-1970s, and the departure of Rwigyema to an unknown location, led to a decline in his academic performance and an increased tendency to fight those who belittled the Rwandan population.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200814-17) He was eventually suspended from Ntare and completed his studies at Old Kampala Secondary School.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200815-18)

After completing his education, Kagame made two visits to Rwanda, in 1977 and 1978. He was initially hosted by family members of his former classmates, but upon arrival in [Kigali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kigali "Kigali"), he made contact with members of his own family.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh200416%E2%80%9318-19) He kept a low profile on these visits, believing that his status as a well-connected Tutsi exile could lead to arrest. On his second visit, he entered the country through [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire") rather than Uganda to avoid suspicion.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh200416%E2%80%9318-19) Kagame used his time in Rwanda to explore the country, familiarise himself with the political and social situation, and make connections that would prove useful to him in his later activities.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh200416%E2%80%9318-19)

## Military career, 1979–1994

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career, 1979–1994")]

### Ugandan Bush War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Ugandan Bush War")]

Further information: [Ugandan Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugandan_Bush_War "Ugandan Bush War")

[![Image 8: Profile picture of Yoweri Museveni during a visit to President Reagan of the United States in 1987](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f3/Museveni1987.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Museveni1987.png)

Kagame served under [Yoweri Museveni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoweri_Museveni "Yoweri Museveni") (pictured) in the [Ugandan Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugandan_Bush_War "Ugandan Bush War").

In 1978, [Fred Rwigyema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Rwigyema "Fred Rwigyema") returned to western Uganda and reunited with Kagame.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200819-20) During his absence, Rwigyema had joined the rebel army of [Yoweri Museveni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoweri_Museveni "Yoweri Museveni"). Based in [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania"), it aimed to overthrow the Ugandan government of [Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idi_Amin "Idi Amin").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200819-20) Rwigyema returned to Tanzania and fought in [the 1979 war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda%E2%80%93Tanzania_War "Uganda–Tanzania War") during which Museveni's rebel group, [FRONASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_for_National_Salvation "Front for National Salvation"), allied with the Tanzanian army and other Ugandan exiles, defeated Amin.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEState_House,_Republic_of_Uganda-21) After Amin's defeat, Kagame and other Rwandan refugees pledged allegiance to Museveni, who had become a cabinet member in the transition government.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200820-22) Kagame received training at the [United States Army Command and General Staff College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Command_and_General_Staff_College "United States Army Command and General Staff College"), [Fort Leavenworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Leavenworth "Fort Leavenworth"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200838%E2%80%9339-23)

Former incumbent [Milton Obote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Obote "Milton Obote") won the [1980 Ugandan general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Ugandan_general_election "1980 Ugandan general election"). Museveni disputed the result, and he and his followers withdrew from the new government in protest. In 1981, Museveni formed the rebel [Popular Resistance Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Resistance_Army "Popular Resistance Army") (PRA); Kagame and Rwigyema joined as founding soldiers, along with 38 Ugandans.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAssociated_Press_(I)1981-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200839-25) The army's goal was to overthrow Obote's government, in what became known as the Ugandan Bush War.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200839-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTENganda2009-26) Kagame took part in the [Battle of Kabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kabamba "Battle of Kabamba"), the PRA's first operation, in February 1981.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKainerugaba201067%E2%80%9368,_76-27)

Kagame and Rwigema joined the PRA primarily to ease conditions for Rwandan refugees persecuted by Obote. They also had a long-term goal of returning with other Tutsi refugees to Rwanda; military experience would enable them to fight the Hutu-dominated Rwandan army.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200840-28) The PRA merged with another rebel group in June 1981, forming the [National Resistance Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Resistance_Army "National Resistance Army") (NRA).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKasozi1994164%E2%80%93165-29) In the NRA, Kagame specialized in intelligence-gathering, and he rose to a position close to Museveni's.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200844%E2%80%9345-30) The NRA, based in the [Luwero Triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luwero_Triangle "Luwero Triangle"), fought the Ugandan army for the next five years, even after Obote was deposed in [a 1985 coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Ugandan_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1985 Ugandan coup d'état") and the start of [peace talks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_Agreement,_1985 "Nairobi Agreement, 1985").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTELibrary_of_Congress2010-31)

In 1986, the NRA [captured Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kampala "Battle of Kampala") with a force of 14,000 soldiers, including 500 Rwandans, and formed a new government.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200847-32) After Museveni's inauguration as president he appointed Kagame and Rwigyema as senior officers in the new Ugandan army; Kagame was the head of military intelligence.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200850%E2%80%9351-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson_(I)2000-34) In a 2018 paper, Canadian scholar and Rwanda expert [Gerald Caplan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Caplan "Gerald Caplan") described this appointment as a remarkable achievement for a foreigner and a refugee. Caplan noted Museveni's reputation for toughness, and said that Kagame would have had to be similarly tough to earn such a position. He also commented on the nature of military intelligence work, saying "it is surely unrealistic to expect that Kagame refrained from the kind of unsavory activities that military security specializes in."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018153-35) In addition to their army duties, Kagame and Rwigyema began building a covert network of Rwandan Tutsi refugees within the army's ranks, intended as the nucleus for an attack on Rwanda.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200851%E2%80%9352-36) In 1989, Rwanda's President [Habyarimana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juv%C3%A9nal_Habyarimana "Juvénal Habyarimana") and many Ugandans in the army began to criticise Museveni over his appointment of Rwandan refugees to senior positions,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMamdani2002175-37) and he demoted Kagame and Rwigyema.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200853-38)

Kagame and Rwigyema remained _de facto_ senior officers, but the change caused them to accelerate their plans to invade Rwanda.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200853%E2%80%9354-39) They joined an organisation called the [Rwandan Patriotic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Patriotic_Front "Rwandan Patriotic Front") (RPF), a refugee association which had been operating under various names since 1979.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200848%E2%80%9350-40) Rwigyema became the RPF leader shortly after joining and, while still working for the Ugandan army, he and Kagame completed their invasion plans.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer200854-41)

### Rwandan Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rwandan Civil War")]

Further information: [Rwandan Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Civil_War "Rwandan Civil War")

[![Image 9: Photograph of a lake with one of the Virunga Mountains behind, partially in cloud](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/RwandaVolcanoAndLake_cropped2.jpg/250px-RwandaVolcanoAndLake_cropped2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RwandaVolcanoAndLake_cropped2.jpg)

The [Virunga Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virunga_Mountains "Virunga Mountains"), Kagame's RPF base from 1990 to 1991

In October 1990, Rwigyema led a force of over 4,000[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMelvern200614-42) RPF rebels into Rwanda at the [Kagitumba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kagitumba "Kagitumba") border post, advancing 60 km (37 mi) south to the town of Gabiro.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier199994%E2%80%9395-43) Kagame was not present at the initial raids, as he was in the United States, attending the [Command and General Staff College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Command_and_General_Staff_College "United States Army Command and General Staff College") in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. On the second day of the attack, Rwigyema was shot in the head and killed.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018153-35) The exact circumstances are disputed; the official line of Kagame's government,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGovernment_of_Rwanda2009-44) and the version mentioned by historian [Gérard Prunier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A9rard_Prunier "Gérard Prunier") in his 1995 book on the subject, was that Rwigyema was killed by a stray bullet.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier199995%E2%80%9396-45)

In his 2009 book _Africa's World War_, Prunier says Rwigyema was killed by his subcommander Peter Bayingana, following an argument over tactics. According to this account, Bayingana and fellow subcommander Chris Bunyenyezi were then executed on the orders of Museveni.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier200913%E2%80%9314-46) In a 2005 conversation with Caplan, Prunier provided a different account, stating that Bayingana and Bunyenyezi's killers were recruited by Kagame. Caplan notes that lack of research means the truth of this is uncertain, but that if true, the "tales of death and intrigue [offer] yet another insight into Kagame's character".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018153-35) Rwigyema's death threw the RPF into confusion. France and Zaire deployed forces in support of the Rwandan army, and by the end of October, the RPF had been pushed back into the far north east corner of the country.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier199996-47)

Kagame returned to Africa and took command of the RPF forces, which had been reduced to fewer than 2,000 troops.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMelvern200027%E2%80%9330-48) Kagame and his soldiers moved west, through Uganda, to the [Virunga Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virunga_Mountains "Virunga Mountains"), a rugged high-altitude area where the terrain worked in their favour.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999114%E2%80%93115-49) From there, he re-armed and reorganised the army, and carried out fundraising and recruitment from the Tutsi diaspora.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999117%E2%80%93118-50) Kagame restarted combat in January 1991, with an attack on the northern town of [Ruhengeri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruhengeri "Ruhengeri"). Benefiting from the element of surprise, the RPF captured the town and held it for a day before retreating back into the forests.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999120-51)

For the next year, the RPF waged a hit-and-run [guerrilla war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_war "Guerrilla war"), capturing some border areas but not making significant gains against the Rwandan army. These actions caused an exodus of around 300,000 Hutu from the affected areas.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999135-52) Prunier wrote in 1995 that the RPF were surprised that Hutu peasants "showed no enthusiasm for being 'liberated' by them".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999136-53) In her 2018 book _[In Praise of Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Praise\_of\_Blood "In Praise of Blood")_, however, Canadian journalist [Judi Rever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judi_Rever "Judi Rever") quoted witnesses who said that the exodus was forced by RPF attacks on the villages including the laying of landmines and shooting of children. Caplan's paper questions the credibility of many of the witnesses Rever had spoken to, but noted that "there are considerable other sources besides Rever that attest to RPF war crimes".[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018178%E2%80%93180-54)

Following the June 1992 formation of a multi-party coalition government in Kigali, Kagame announced a ceasefire and initiated negotiations with the Rwandan government in [Arusha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arusha "Arusha"), Tanzania.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999150-55) In early-1993, groups of extremist Hutu formed and began campaigns of large-scale violence against the Tutsi.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999173%E2%80%93174-56) Kagame responded by suspending peace talks temporarily and launching a major attack, gaining a large swathe of land across the north of the country.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999174%E2%80%93177-57)

Peace negotiations resumed in Arusha, and the resulting set of agreements, known as the [Arusha Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arusha_Accords_(Rwanda) "Arusha Accords (Rwanda)"), were signed in August 1993. The RPF were given positions in a broad-based transitional government (BBTG) and in the national army.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999187,_190%E2%80%93191-58) The [United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Assistance_Mission_for_Rwanda "United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda") (UNAMIR), a peacekeeping force, arrived and the RPF were given a base in the [national parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Rwanda "Parliament of Rwanda") building in Kigali to use during the establishment of the BBTG.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005126%E2%80%93131-59)

### Rwandan genocide

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Rwandan genocide")]

Main article: [Rwandan genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide")

On 6 April 1994, Rwandan President Habyarimana's plane [was shot down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Juv%C3%A9nal_Habyarimana_and_Cyprien_Ntaryamira "Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira") near [Kigali Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kigali_Airport "Kigali Airport"), killing both Habyarimana and the [President of Burundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Presidents_of_Burundi "List of Presidents of Burundi"), [Cyprien Ntaryamira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprien_Ntaryamira "Cyprien Ntaryamira"), as well as their entourage and three French crew members.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTENational_Assembly_of_France1998-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(I)2010-61) The attackers remain unknown. Prunier, in his 1995 book, concluded that it was most likely a coup d'état carried out by extreme Hutu members of Habyarimana's government who feared that the president was serious about honouring the Arusha agreement, and was a planned part of the genocide.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999221-62) This theory was disputed in 2006 by French judge [Jean-Louis Bruguière](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Louis_Brugui%C3%A8re "Jean-Louis Bruguière"), and in 2008 by Spanish judge [Fernando Andreu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Andreu "Fernando Andreu").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilkinson2008-63) Both alleged that Kagame and the RPF were responsible.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrugui%C3%A8re20061-64)

Rever also held Kagame responsible, giving as his motive a desire to plunge Rwanda into disorder and therefore provide a platform for the RPF to complete their conquest of the country. Evaluating the two arguments later in 2018, Caplan questioned the evidence used by Bruguière and Rever, stating that it has been repeatedly "discredited for its methodology and its dependence on sources who have split bitterly with Kagame".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018176-65) Caplan also noted that Hutu extremists had made multiple prior threats to kill Habyarimana in their journals and radio stations, and cited eyewitness accounts of roadblocks being erected in Kigali and killings initiated within one hour of the crash – evidence that the shooting of the plane was ordered as the initiation of the genocide.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018177%E2%80%93178-66)

Following Habyarimana's death, a military committee led by Colonel [Théoneste Bagosora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9oneste_Bagosora "Théoneste Bagosora") took immediate control of the country.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005224-67) Under the committee's direction, the Hutu militia [Interahamwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interahamwe "Interahamwe") and the Presidential Guard began to kill Hutu and Tutsi opposition politicians and other prominent Tutsi figures.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999230-68) The killers then targeted the entire Tutsi population, as well as moderate Hutu,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTERombouts2004182-69) beginning the [Rwandan genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_New_York_Times1994-70) Over the course of approximately 100 days, an estimated 206,000 to 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu were killed on the orders of the committee.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeierhenrich2020-71)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuichaoua20203-72) On 7 April, Kagame warned the committee and UNAMIR that he would resume the civil war if the killing did not stop.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005247-73)

The next day, the Rwandan government forces attacked the national parliament building from several directions, but the RPF troops stationed there successfully fought back.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005264%E2%80%93265-74) Kagame began an attack from the north on three fronts, seeking to link up quickly with the troops isolated in Kigali.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005269-75) An interim government was set up but Kagame refused to talk to it, believing that it was just a cover for Bagosora's rule.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999268-76) Over the next few days, the RPF advanced steadily south, capturing Gabiro and large areas of countryside to the north and east of Kigali.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005288-77) They avoided attacking Kigali or [Byumba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byumba "Byumba") at this stage, but conducted manoeuvres designed to encircle the cities and cut off supply routes.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005299-78)

Throughout April there were numerous attempts by UNAMIR to establish a ceasefire, but Kagame insisted each time that the RPF would not stop fighting unless the killings stopped.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005300-79) In late April, the RPF secured the whole of the Tanzanian border area and began to move west from Kibungo, to the south of Kigali.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005326%E2%80%93327-80) They encountered little resistance, except around Kigali and Ruhengeri.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999268-76) By 16 May, they had cut the road between Kigali and [Gitarama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gitarama "Gitarama"), the temporary home of the interim government, and by 13 June, they had taken Gitarama, following an unsuccessful attempt by the Rwandan government forces to reopen the road. The interim government was forced to relocate to [Gisenyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gisenyi "Gisenyi") in the far north west.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005410-81) As well as fighting the war, Kagame was recruiting heavily to expand the army. The new recruits included Tutsi survivors of the genocide and refugees from [Burundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burundi "Burundi"), but were less well trained and disciplined than the earlier recruits.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999270-82)

Having completed the encirclement of Kigali, Kagame spent the latter half of June fighting to take the city.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005421-83) The government forces had superior manpower and weapons, but the RPF steadily gained territory, as well as conducting raids to rescue civilians from behind enemy lines.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005421-83) According to [Roméo Dallaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rom%C3%A9o_Dallaire "Roméo Dallaire"), the force commander of UNAMIR, this success was due to Kagame being a "master of psychological warfare";[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005421-83) he exploited the fact that the government forces were concentrating on the genocide rather than the fight for Kigali, and capitalised on the government's loss of morale as it lost territory.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005421-83) The RPF finally defeated the Rwandan government forces in Kigali on 4 July,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005459-84) and on 18 July took Gisenyi and the rest of the north west, forcing the interim government into Zaire and ending the genocide.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999298%E2%80%93299-85) At the end of July 1994, Kagame's forces held the whole of Rwanda except for a zone in the south west, which had been occupied by a French-led United Nations force as part of _[Opération Turquoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Op%C3%A9ration\_Turquoise "Opération Turquoise")_.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDallaire2005474%E2%80%93475-86)

Kagame's tactics and actions during the genocide have proved controversial. Western observers such as Dallaire and [Luc Marchal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luc_Marchal "Luc Marchal"), the senior Belgian peacekeeper in Rwanda at the time, have stated that the RPF prioritised taking power over saving lives or stopping the genocide.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-89) Scholars also believe that the RPF killed many Rwandan civilians, predominantly Hutu, during the genocide and in the months that followed. The death toll from these killings is in the tens or even hundreds of thousands.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999359%E2%80%93360-90) In her book _Leave None to Tell the Story: Genocide in Rwanda_, written for [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch"), Rwanda expert [Alison des Forges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alison_des_Forges "Alison des Forges") wrote that despite saving many lives, the RPF "relentlessly pursued those whom they thought guilty of genocide" and that "in their drive for military victory and a halt to the genocide, the RPF killed thousands, including noncombatants as well as government troops and members of militia".[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDes_Forges1999691-91)

Human rights violations by the RPF during the genocide have also been documented in a 2000 report compiled by the [Organisation of African Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity "Organisation of African Unity"), and by Prunier in _Africa's World War_.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018155%E2%80%93157-92) In an interview with journalist [Stephen Kinzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Kinzer "Stephen Kinzer"), Kagame acknowledged that killings had occurred but said that they were carried out by rogue soldiers and had been impossible to control.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008191-93) RPF killings continued after the end of the genocide, gaining international attention with the 1995 [Kibeho massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibeho_massacre "Kibeho massacre"), in which soldiers opened fire on a camp for [internally displaced persons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internally_displaced_persons "Internally displaced persons") in [Butare Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butare_Province "Butare Province").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTELorch1995-94) Australian soldiers serving as part of UNAMIR estimated at least 4,000 people were killed,[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAustralian_War_Memorial-95) while the Rwandan government claimed that the death toll was 338.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier200942-96)

## Vice President and Minister of Defence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Vice President and Minister of Defence")]

The post-genocide Rwandan government took office in Kigali in July 1994.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999299-97) It was based loosely on the Arusha Accords, but Habyarimana's party, MRND was outlawed. The positions it had been assigned were taken over by the RPF.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999299%E2%80%93300-98) The military wing of the RPF was renamed as the [Rwandan Patriotic Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Patriotic_Army "Rwandan Patriotic Army") (RPA), and became the national army.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWallis2007ix-99) Paul Kagame assumed the dual roles of [Vice President of Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_Rwanda "Vice President of Rwanda") and [Minister of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Defence_(Rwanda) "Minister of Defence (Rwanda)") while [Pasteur Bizimungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteur_Bizimungu "Pasteur Bizimungu"), a Hutu who had been a civil servant under Habyarimana before fleeing to join the RPF, was appointed president.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier199990,_300-100) Bizimungu and his cabinet had some control over domestic affairs, but Kagame remained commander-in-chief of the army and was the de facto ruler of the country.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh2004120%E2%80%93121-101)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999369-102) German public broadcaster [Deutsche Welle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Welle "Deutsche Welle") stated that "Bizimungu was commonly seen as a placeholder for Kagame".[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeutsche_Welle2020-103)

### Domestic situation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Domestic situation")]

[![Image 10: Overhead view of Kagame and Perry seated on leather seats with a large microphone visible and another army member in the background](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/DF-ST-98-01731.jpg/250px-DF-ST-98-01731.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DF-ST-98-01731.jpg)

Vice President Kagame with United States Secretary of Defense [William J. Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Perry "William J. Perry"), July 1994

The infrastructure and economy of the country suffered greatly during the genocide. Many buildings were uninhabitable, and the former regime had taken all currency and moveable assets when they fled the country.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008181-104) Human resources were also severely depleted, with over 40% of the population having been killed or fled.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008181-104) Many who remained were traumatised; most had lost relatives, witnessed killings, or participated in the genocide.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnited_States_Holocaust_Memorial_Museum-105) Kagame controlled the national army and was responsible for maintaining the government's power, while other officials began rebuilding the country.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonner1994-106)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008187-107)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDepartment_of_State_(VI)1995-108)

[Non-governmental organisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization "Non-governmental organization") began to move back into the country, and the [international community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_community "International community") spent US$1.5 billion on [humanitarian aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanitarian_aid "Humanitarian aid") between July and December 1994, but Prunier described this as "largely unconnected with the real economic needs of the community".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999327%E2%80%93328-109) Kagame strove to portray the government as inclusive and not Tutsi-dominated. He directed removal of ethnicity from citizens' national identity cards, and the government began a policy of downplaying the distinctions between Hutu, Tutsi, and Twa.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonner1994-106)

The unity government suffered a partial collapse in 1995. The continuing violence, along with appointing of local government officials who were almost exclusively RPF Tutsi, caused serious disagreement between Kagame and senior Hutu government members, including prime minister [Faustin Twagiramungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faustin_Twagiramungu "Faustin Twagiramungu") and interior minister [Seth Sendashonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_Sendashonga "Seth Sendashonga").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999367%E2%80%93368-110) Twagiramungu resigned in August, and Kagame fired Sendashonga and three others the next day.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999367%E2%80%93368-110) Pasteur Bizimungu remained president but the makeup of the new government was predominantly RPF Tutsi loyal to Kagame.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008192-111)

Twagiramungu and Sendashonga moved abroad to form a new opposition party shortly after leaving the government.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999368-112) Sendashonga, who had also spoken out about the need for punishing killings by rogue RPF soldiers, moved to Kenya. Having survived an attempt on his life in 1996, he was assassinated in Nairobi in May 1998, when a UN vehicle in which he was travelling was fired upon.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies1998-113) Many observers believe Kagame ordered the killing; as Caplan noted: "the RPF denied any responsibility, which no one other than RPF partisans believed".[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018158-114)

### Refugee crisis and insurgency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Refugee crisis and insurgency")]

Main article: [Great Lakes refugee crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_refugee_crisis "Great Lakes refugee crisis")

[![Image 11: View of refugee camp on foggy day, showing tents of various colours and the refugees](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Rwandan_refugee_camp_in_east_Zaire.jpg/250px-Rwandan_refugee_camp_in_east_Zaire.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rwandan_refugee_camp_in_east_Zaire.jpg)

A [refugee camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_camp "Refugee camp") in [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire"), 1994

Following the RPF victory, approximately two million Hutu fled to refugee camps in neighboring countries, particularly Zaire, fearing RPF reprisals for the Rwandan genocide.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999312-115) The camps were set up by the [United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_High_Commissioner_for_Refugees "United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees") (UNHCR), but were effectively controlled by the army and government of the former Hutu regime, including many leaders of the genocide.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999313%E2%80%93314-116) This regime was determined to return to power in Rwanda and began rearming, killing Tutsi residing in Zaire, and launching cross-border incursions in conjunction with the _Interahamwe_ paramilitary group.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999381%E2%80%93382-117)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPomfret1997-118) By late 1996, the Hutu militants represented a serious threat to the new Rwandan regime, and Kagame launched a counteroffensive.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999382-119)

Kagame first provided troops and military training[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPomfret1997-118) to aid a rebellion against Zaire by the [Banyamulenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banyamulenge "Banyamulenge"), a Tutsi group living near [Bukavu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukavu "Bukavu") in the Zairian [South Kivu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Kivu "South Kivu") province.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999384%E2%80%93385-120) With Rwandan army support, the Banyamulenge defeated local security forces and began attacking the Hutu refugee camps in the area. At the same time, Kagame's forces joined with Zairian Tutsi around [Goma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goma "Goma") to attack two of the camps there.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPomfret1997-118)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier1999384%E2%80%93385-120) Most refugees from the attacked camps moved to the large Mugunga camp. In November 1996, the Rwandan army attacked Mugunga, causing an estimated 800,000 refugees to flee.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009118-121) Many returned to Rwanda despite the presence of the RPF; others ventured further west into Zaire.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009122%E2%80%93123-122)

Despite the disbanding of the camps, the defeated forces of the former regime continued a cross-border insurgency campaign into Rwanda from [North Kivu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Kivu "North Kivu").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008209-123) The insurgents maintained a presence in Rwanda's north western provinces and were supported by the predominantly Hutu population, many of whom had lived in the refugee camps before they were attacked.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008216-124) In addition to supporting the wars in the Congo, Kagame began a propaganda campaign to bring the Hutu to his side.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008215%E2%80%93218-125) He integrated former soldiers of the deposed genocidal regime's military into the RPF-dominated [national army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Defence_Forces "Rwandan Defence Forces") and appointed senior Hutu to key local government positions in the areas hit by insurgency.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008215%E2%80%93218-125) These tactics were eventually successful; by 1999, the population in the north west had stopped supporting the insurgency and the insurgents were mostly defeated.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrittain1999-126)

### Congo wars

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Congo wars")]

Main articles: [First Congo War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Congo_War "First Congo War") and [Second Congo War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Congo_War "Second Congo War")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Second_Congo_War_Africa_map_en.png/250px-Second_Congo_War_Africa_map_en.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Second_Congo_War_Africa_map_en.png)

Belligerents of the [Second Congo War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Congo_War "Second Congo War")

Although his primary reason for military action in Zaire was the dismantling of the refugee camps, Kagame also began planning a war to remove long-time dictator President [Mobutu Sese Seko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobutu_Sese_Seko "Mobutu Sese Seko") from power.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPomfret1997-118) Mobutu had supported the _genocidaires_ based in the camps, and was also accused of allowing attacks on Tutsi people within Zaire.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBymanChalkHoffmanRosenau200118-127) Together with Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, Kagame supported the newly created [Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_of_Democratic_Forces_for_the_Liberation_of_Congo "Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo") (ADFL), an alliance of four rebel groups headed by [Laurent-Désiré Kabila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent-D%C3%A9sir%C3%A9_Kabila "Laurent-Désiré Kabila"), which began waging the [First Congo War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Congo_War "First Congo War").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009113%E2%80%93116-128)

The ADFL, helped by Rwandan and Ugandan troops, took control of North and South Kivu provinces in November 1996 and then advanced west, gaining territory from the poorly organised and demotivated Zairian army with little fighting.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009128%E2%80%93133-129) By May 1997, they controlled almost the whole of Zaire except for the capital [Kinshasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa "Kinshasa"); Mobutu fled and the ADFL took the capital without fighting.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009136-130) The country was renamed as the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo") (DRC) and Kabila became the new president.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(II)-131) The [Rwandan Defence Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_Defence_Forces "Rwandan Defence Forces") and the [ADFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_of_Democratic_Forces_for_the_Liberation_of_Congo "Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo") were accused of carrying out mass atrocities during the First Congo War, with as many as 222,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees declared missing.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECDI1998-132)

Kagame and the Rwandan government retained strong influence over Kabila following his inauguration, and the RPA maintained a heavy presence in Kinshasa.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009174-133) Congolese in the capital resented this, as did many in the eastern Kivu provinces, where ethnic clashes increased sharply.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009177-134) In July 1998, Kabila fired his Rwandan chief-of-staff, [James Kabarebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Kabarebe "James Kabarebe"), and ordered all RPA troops to leave the country.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009178%E2%80%93179-135) Kagame accused Kabila of supporting the ongoing insurgency against Rwanda from North Kivu, the same accusation he had made about Mobutu.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008210%E2%80%93211-136) He responded to the expulsion of his soldiers by backing a new rebel group, the [Rally for Congolese Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rally_for_Congolese_Democracy "Rally for Congolese Democracy") (RCD), and launching the [Second Congo War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Congo_War "Second Congo War").[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009182%E2%80%93183-137)

The first action of the war was a [blitzkrieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blitzkrieg "Blitzkrieg") by the RCD and RPA, led by Kabarebe. These forces made quick gains, advancing in twelve days from the Kivu provinces west to within 130 kilometres (81 mi) of Kinshasa.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009184-138) The capital was saved by the intervention of [Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angola "Angola"), Namibia and [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe") on Kabila's side.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009186-139) Following the failure of the blitzkrieg, the conflict developed into a long-term conventional war, which lasted until 2003 and caused millions of deaths and massive damage.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(II)-131) According to a report by the [International Rescue Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Rescue_Committee "International Rescue Committee") (IRC), this conflict led to the loss of between 3 million and 7.6 million lives, many through starvation and disease accompanying the social disruption of the war.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAssociated_Press_(II)2010-140)

Although Kagame's primary reason for the two wars in the Congo was Rwanda's security, he was alleged to gain economic benefit by exploiting the [mineral wealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_industry_of_the_Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Mining industry of the Democratic Republic of the Congo") of the eastern Congo.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008211%E2%80%93212-141) The 2001 United Nations _Report of the Panel of Experts on the Illegal Exploitation of Natural Resources and Other Forms of Wealth of the Democratic Republic of the Congo_ alleged that Kagame, along with Ugandan President Museveni, were "on the verge of becoming the godfathers of the illegal exploitation of natural resources and the continuation of the conflict in the Democratic Republic of the Congo".[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnited_Nations_(IV)2001211-142) The report also claimed that the Rwandan Ministry of Defence contained a "Congo Desk" dedicated to collecting taxes from companies licensed to mine minerals around [Kisangani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisangani "Kisangani"), and that substantial quantities of [coltan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coltan "Coltan") and diamonds passed through Kigali before being resold on the international market by staff on the Congo Desk.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnited_Nations_(IV)2001126%E2%80%93129-143)

International NGO [Global Witness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Witness "Global Witness") also conducted field studies in early 2013. It concluded that minerals from North and South Kivu are exported illegally to Rwanda and then marketed as Rwandan.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlobal_Witness20136-144) Kagame dismissed these allegations as unsubstantiated and politically motivated; in a 2002 interview with newsletter _[Africa Confidential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa\_Confidential "Africa Confidential"),_ Kagame said that if solid evidence against Rwandan officers was presented, it would be dealt with very seriously.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithWallis2002-145) In 2010, the United Nations released a report accusing the Rwandan army of committing wide scale human rights violations and crimes against humanity in the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the [First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Congo_War "First Congo War") and [Second Congo Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Congo_War "Second Congo War"), charges denied by the Rwandan government.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcGreal2010-146)

## Presidency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Presidency")]

### Accession

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Accession")]

In the late 1990s, Kagame began to disagree publicly with Bizimungu and the Hutu-led government in Rwanda.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008220,_240%E2%80%93241-147) Kagame accused Bizimungu of corruption and poor management,[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008221%E2%80%93222-148) while Bizimungu felt that he had no power over appointments to the cabinet and that the [Transitional National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitional_National_Assembly_of_Rwanda "Transitional National Assembly of Rwanda") was acting purely as a puppet for Kagame.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009241-149) Bizimungu resigned from the presidency in March 2000.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(III)2000-150) Historians generally believe that Bizimungu was forced into resigning by Kagame after denouncing the National Assembly and attempting to sow discord within the RPF.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrunier2009241-149)[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaplan2018161-151) However, Kagame told Kinzer that he was surprised by the development saying that he had received the "startling news" in a phone call from a friend.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008224-152) Following Bizimungu's resignation, the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Rwanda "Supreme Court of Rwanda") ruled that Kagame should become acting president until a permanent successor was chosen.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIRIN_(I)2000-153)

Kagame had been de facto leader since 1994, but focused more on military, foreign affairs and the country's security than day-to-day governance. By 2000, the threat posed by cross-border rebels was reduced and when Bizimungu resigned, Kagame decided to seek the presidency himself.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008220-154) The transitional constitution was still in effect, which meant the president was elected by government ministers and the Transitional National Assembly rather than by a [direct election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_election "Direct election").[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnited_Nations_(V)-155)

The RPF selected two candidates, Kagame and RPF secretary general [Charles Murigande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Murigande "Charles Murigande"); the ministers and parliament elected Kagame by eighty-one votes to three.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(IV)2000-156) Kagame was sworn in as president in April 2000.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(V)2000-157) Several Hutu politicians, including the prime minister [Pierre-Célestin Rwigema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-C%C3%A9lestin_Rwigema "Pierre-Célestin Rwigema"), left the government at around the same time as Bizimungu, leaving a cabinet dominated by those close to Kagame.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKinzer2008224-152) Bizimungu started his own party in 2001, but Kagame's government banned it on the grounds that political campaigning was not permitted under the transitional constitution. The following year, Kagame issued a public statement to Bizimungu, warning him that the government's patience with his continued involvement in party politics was "not infinite",[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-:1-158) and Bizimungu was arrested two weeks later[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIRIN_(V)2002-159) and convicted of corruption and inciting ethnic violence, charges which human rights groups said were politically motivated.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAsiimwe2007-160) He was imprisoned until 2007, when he was [pardoned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative_of_mercy_(Rwanda) "Prerogative of mercy (Rwanda)") by Kagame.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(VI)2007-161)

### New constitution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kagame&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: New constitution")]

Main article: [Constitution of Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Rwanda "Constitution of Rwanda")

Between 1994 and 2003, Rwanda was governed by a set of documents combining President Habyarimana's 1991 constitution, the Arusha Accords, and some additional protocols introduced by the transitional government.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGasamagera20071%E2%80%932-162) As required by the accords, Kagame set up a constitutional commission to draft a new permanent constitution.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGasamagera20073-163) The constitution was required to adhere to a set of fundamental principles including equitable power sharing and democracy.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGasamagera20074-164) The commission sought to ensure that the draft constitution was "home-grown", relevant to Rwanda's specific needs, and reflected the views of the entire population; they sent questionnaires to civil groups across the country and rejected offers of help from the international community, except for financial assistance.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGasamagera20075%E2%80%936-165)

The draft constitution was released in 2003; it was approved by the parliament, and was then put to a referendum in May of that year.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBBC_News_(VII)2003-166) The referendum was widely promoted by the government; ultimately, 95% of eligible adults registered to vote and the turnout on voting day was 87%.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEconomist2003-167) The constitution was overwhelmingly accepted, with 93% voting in favour.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEconomist2003-167) The constitution provided for a two-house parliament, an elected president serving seven-year terms, and multi-party politics.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEconomist2003-167)
